analysis.one_liner: Creates automatic, online, and same-day voter registration and guarantees early, mail, and paper-ballot voting nationwide.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: introduced in September 2024 with 14 cosponsors, it sat in six House committees until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would set nationwide standards for how Americans register and vote. It would require states to automatically register eligible people through government agencies (with an opt-out), offer online registration and updates, allow same-day registration, guarantee early voting, provide no-excuse voting by mail, and require voter-verified paper ballots. It would also expand voting access for people with disabilities, protect voters from deceptive practices and intimidation, restore federal voting rights to citizens after they finish a criminal sentence, and provide grants to states to cover the costs.
analysis.who_benefits: Eligible voters who face barriers under today's patchwork system: people who move and lose their registration, young people, people with disabilities, voters in states without early or mail voting, and citizens who have completed a criminal sentence and had their voting rights taken away. Registration would largely happen automatically through agencies people already interact with, and every state would have to offer online registration, same-day registration, at least early voting, no-excuse mail voting, and a paper trail.

how_it_helps.text: Every state would have to automatically register eligible individuals to vote using information transferred from government agencies such as motor vehicle authorities, Medicaid, the Social Security Administration, and the VA, unless the person affirmatively declines.
States would have to offer online voter registration and let registered voters update their address or information online, with confirmation notices by mail, email, or text.
Every state would have to allow same-day registration on election day and during early voting, and cast a regular ballot at the polls.
States would have to guarantee early voting and no-excuse voting by mail, including secured drop boxes, ballot tracking, and prepaid postage for voting materials.

States would have to use voter-verified permanent paper ballots and manual counting requirements, and states could not remove voters from the rolls based on interstate cross-checks unless they matched full name, date of birth, and the last four digits of a Social Security number, or obtained documentation from the ERIC system.

The bill would bar deceptive practices (such as false information about when, where, and how to vote) and voter caging-based challenges, prohibit hindering voter registration, and impose safeguards for voters with disabilities, older voters, voters on Indian lands, and voters subject to guardianship.

Citizens who have completed a criminal sentence would have their right to vote in federal elections restored, with notification of that restoration, paid for in part through reductions in federal prison funds.

States could not require more than the last four digits of a Social Security number on voter registration applications, and could not require an ID that a voter cannot meet when a sworn written statement is offered instead.

analysis.who_pays: State and local election offices would bear the cost of building automatic, online, and same-day registration systems and meeting new ballot and access requirements, offset by $500 million in authorized federal grants for fiscal year 2025 plus additional sums in later years. Election technology vendors that sell paperless voting machines would lose sales under the paper-ballot requirements, and commercial data brokers would be barred from using registration data for commercial purposes. Federal taxpayers would fund the grants, and federal prison funding would be reduced to help cover the voting-rights restoration.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes $500 million in grants for fiscal 2025 and 'such sums as may be necessary' after that, so states would still shoulder ongoing costs of running automatic registration and expanded voting systems beyond the federal funding.

Automatic registration through agencies including Medicaid, firearm-regulating agencies, and high schools would transfer personal data from many agencies to election officials, which raises privacy and data-security concerns even though the bill imposes NIST security standards and bars commercial use of the data.

The bill imposes federal mandates on how all 50 states run their own elections, which opponents of federal election standards would object to as an intrusion on state election administration; the effective dates also give states waivers that could delay compliance to 2027 or 2028.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are broad: tens of millions of eligible Americans are unregistered or purged, and the bill removes the main bureaucratic barriers — deadlines, paperwork, ID mismatches, and mail-based purges — while adding paper-ballot integrity protections. The costs are real but modest relative to a federal election system: state implementation expenses, ongoing grant appropriations, and genuine privacy questions about agency data-sharing, which the bill addresses with security standards and data-use limits. The main criticism is not that the trade is bad but that it was never actually tested by a debate or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late September 2024, referred to six House committees, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. James Clyburn introduced the Voter Empowerment Act of 2024 in the House on September 20, 2024, late in the second session of the 118th Congress.
The same day, it was referred to six committees: House Administration, Judiciary, Oversight and Accountability, Science, Space, and Technology, Education and the Workforce, and Energy and Commerce.
Fourteen House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsor appears in the record.
No committee reported the bill and the full action history shows no further action after the referrals, so it died in committee when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
Because it was never debated or voted on, no lawmaker ever went on record supporting or opposing its substance on the floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State election systems remain exactly as they were, so the main beneficiaries of the bill's death are state officials and election technology vendors who did not have to change anything. Americans who face registration deadlines, purges, or no early or mail voting gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State election officials and vendors, unchanged

for.name: Rep. James E. Clyburn
for.role: Sponsor, Assistant Democratic Leader (42nd district-scalar: senior House Democrat from South Carolina)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the House in September 2024.

against.name: Speaker of the House (Mike Johnson)
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to committees 'for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker' and was never scheduled for committee or floor action; the Congress ended with no vote.

against.name: Chairs of the six referred committees
against.role: Committee chairs, House Administration, Judiciary, Oversight, Science, Education and Workforce, Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: None of the six committees held a hearing or reported the bill, per the complete action history.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 recorded supporters (the sponsor plus 14 cosponsors) were House Democrats, and the Republican-controlled House took no action on the bill before the Congress ended.

industries.note: The bill would require voter-verified permanent paper ballots and manual counting requirements, shrinking the market for paperless touchscreen machines these companies sell to states. Ordinary voters get a verifiable ballot trail; vendors lose the paperless product line.
The bill prohibits using voter registration information collected under its automatic registration system for commercial purposes, cutting off a source of personal data these firms profit from.
